question: A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules, is wanted after one last conversion — but it starts with a position trace. A cart's position follows x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous speed at t = 2.0 s is recorded, in meters per second. This speed belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 17000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 26 J is added, then 7 J is added again, then 2 J is added once more, and finally the total is converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two acceleration readings of 6 m/s² and 14 m/s² on a machine test rig are added together and the sum multiplied by 4, giving the machine's effective acceleration. This acts on a part whose mass is stated as 115000 grams. A separate voltage reading of 24 V on the panel is unrelated to this task. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, reduced by 19 kN, scaled by a factor of 5, and finally scaled again by a factor of 9. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a robotic press, the rate at which the ram's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 3t² + 5t (in m/s³, t in seconds); between t = 1 s and t = 2 s, the net change in acceleration has 19 m/s² added to it. This total acceleration acts on the ram, whose mass is stated as 193000 grams. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 6, then reduced by 26 N, and reduced again by 21 N. What is the final force, in newtons?

A conveyor system's final reading, in kilonewtons after a last addition of 28 kN, is the goal — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings of 9 m/s² and 12 m/s² are added and the sum multiplied by 3, giving the conveyor's effective acceleration. This acts on an 88 kg load, producing a force from which 30 N is subtracted. The result is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 9, and finally increased by 28 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a crane test rig, two steel cables measure 351 cm and 244 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a load whose mass is stated as 80000 grams. To the resulting force, 28 N is added, and the total is converted into kilonewtons. From the converted figure, 8 kN is subtracted, and finally the result is scaled by a factor of 7. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A workshop's final force reading, in newtons after a last addition of 10 N, is wanted — but it starts with a batch of test modules. From 6 interchangeable modules on a machine, engineers select groups of 2 for a durability trial; the number of distinct such groups is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a test rig whose mass is stated as 82 kg. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 7, then increased by 20 N, then reduced by 27 N. A separate thermometer reads 26°C, unrelated to this task. Finally, 10 N is added. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in joules after a tenfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 5 and multiply to 6; the smaller is kept as the speed of a 4 kg block on a test bench. A separate stopwatch reads 33 seconds, unrelated to this task. From the block's kinetic energy, 14 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 8, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in joules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a last addition of 15 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 12 and multiply to 32; the larger is kept, and 29 m/s is added to it. This total speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 11000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 6, and finally increased by 15 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two speed values, in m/s, sum to 3 and multiply to 2; the smaller is kept, then 2 m/s is subtracted, and 27 m/s is added back. This net speed belongs to a 3 kg slider on a lab bench. A separate thermometer reads 20°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a machine test rig, two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 6 and multiply to 8; the smaller is kept, then tripled. This acceleration acts on a part whose mass is stated as 97 kg. To the resulting force, 18 N is added, then 4 N is added again, and finally 20 N is added once more. What is the final force, in newtons?

On a vehicle test rig, speed follows v(t) = t³ + 5t² (in m/s, t in seconds); the instantaneous acceleration at t = 1.0 s is recorded. This acceleration acts on the vehicle, whose mass is stated as 75 kg. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 9, then increased by 29 kN, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 9. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A machine's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a threefold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings of 9 m/s² and 4 m/s² are added and the sum multiplied by 4, giving the machine's effective acceleration. This acts on a 28 kg part, producing a force. A separate stopwatch reads 8 seconds, unrelated to this task. The force is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 11, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 3. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test bench, two speed values, in m/s, sum to 9 and multiply to 18; the smaller is kept as the speed of an 18 kg slider. A separate thermometer reads 25°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 11, scaled again by 3, and finally scaled once more by 5. What is the final energy, in joules?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a last addition of 16 kN, is the goal — but it starts with two cable lengths. Two cables measure 363 cm and 326 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is found, and multiplied by 4. This total, used as an acceleration in m/s², acts on a load whose mass is stated as 180000 grams. A separate pressure gauge reads 55 bar, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 7, converted into kilonewtons, and finally increased by 16 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a go-kart test track, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 3 s and t = 4 s, from the area under this graph, belongs to a battery pack whose mass is stated as 24000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 10 J is added, and the total is converted into kilojoules. Finally, 15 kJ is added. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two speed values, in m/s, sum to 13 and multiply to 42; the smaller is kept, then multiplied by 4. This total speed belongs to a 38 kg slider on a lab bench. A separate thermometer reads 18°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 10, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 4. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a crane test rig, two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 10 and multiply to 16; the larger is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is 78 kg. From the resulting force, 6 N is subtracted, then 19 N is added back, and the total is doubled. A separate voltage reading of 110 V on the panel is not needed here. Finally, the force is converted into kilonewtons. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after two successive deductions, is wanted — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 7 and multiply to 10; the smaller is kept as the speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 38000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then reduced by 11 kJ, and reduced again by 29 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test rig, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + 7t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 2 s and t = 3 s, from the area under this graph, has 8 m/s added to it. This total speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 47000 grams. A separate stopwatch reads 40 seconds, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 9, increased by 2 J, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two rods measure 272 cm and 377 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 33000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 14 J is added, then 21 J is subtracted, and finally the total is converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A calibration probe on a lab bench outputs a signal s(t) = t³ + t² over time t in seconds; the second rate of change of this signal at t = 2.0 s is read directly as a speed, in meters per second. This speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 23000 grams. A separate stopwatch reads 55 seconds, unrelated to this task. From the resulting kinetic energy, 16 J is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 10, scaled again by 5, and finally increased by 1 J. What is the final energy, in joules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a last subtraction of 25 kJ, is the goal — but it starts with a series of sensor readings. For each integer k from 1 to 4, a rig logs a reading equal to k²; summing all four readings gives the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 20000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, increased by 12 kJ, scaled by a factor of 6, and finally reduced by 25 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a final subtraction of 9 kN, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 3 and multiply to 2; the smaller is kept, then tripled. This acceleration acts on a load whose mass is 65 kg. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, then increased by 28 kN, and finally reduced by 9 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a last addition of 25 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with two speed readings. Two speeds of 5 m/s and 7 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 6, giving the effective speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 60000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 5, increased by 22 J, converted into kilojoules, and finally increased once more by 25 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test bench, two speeds of 6 m/s and 9 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 4, giving the effective speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 36000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 4, converted into kilojoules, and finally reduced by 27 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?
